newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine says no thanks to Yeltsin's defence offer.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine says no thanks to Yeltsin's defence offer.

text.p: Ukraine's top security official, responding to a promise by Russian President Boris Yeltsin that Moscow would defend its Slav neighbour "in extreme situations", said on Friday that Kiev had not asked for such a guarantee.

"I think President Yeltsin was ruled by his best intentions but there were no requests from the Ukrainian side," Volodymyr Horbulin, Secretary of Ukraine's policy-making Security and Defence Council, told a news conference.
Yeltsin made the offer in an interview broadcast before he left Moscow for Kiev to sign a much-delayed friendship treaty.
"This is in the agreement, that we will participate together to defend Ukraine if anything happens," Yeltsin said.
He did not specify the conditions under which Russia would come to the aid of its fellow ex-Soviet republic.

In the interview, he discussed an accord between Moscow and Kiev dividing the Soviet Black Sea Fleet, over which the two sides had squabbled for years, and allowing Russia to lease naval facilities at the Ukrainian port of Sevastopol.
"I am in favour of us jointly providing security and helping each other in extreme situations, so it is obligatory to help," Yeltsin said.
Ukraine, trying to free itself from centuries of Moscow domination, did not join a Russian-led "collective security pact" within the Commonwealth of Independent States.

Kiev does not share Moscow's opposition to NATO's plans to admit new Eastern European members but on Thursday initialled a pact with the Western defence alliance giving it the right to call for "consultations" if it feels under external threat.
Kiev has no immediate plans to seek NATO membership. "Ukraine is not going to join NATO for now and there are no conditions for that," Horbulin said.
Yeltsin's statement came three days after he signed an agreement with NATO establishing a new security relationship.

The Kremlin leader, who is anxious to prevent former Soviet states from joining NATO, also repeated his warning that Russia would rethink relations with the Western alliance if it sought to expand into the ex-Soviet republics.

"We will reconfirm what I said: if they (NATO leaders) try to drag one of the (ex-Soviet) republics into their sphere as members of NATO, we will re-evaluate our relationship with the alliance," he said. "I've made that clear and can repeat it."
